metaData.originalTitle: 陈嘉映×罗新×周思成：谁在定义真实？
metaData.title: Chen Jiaying × Luo Xin × Zhou Sicheng: Who Defines Reality?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Three scholars, Chen Jiaying, Luo Xin, and Zhou Sicheng, engage in a dialogue on cognition, objectivity, and the value of the humanities in the age of AI, exploring how philosophy and history can help people build their own narratives and judgment amidst fragmented information.
metaData.summary: This article is a transcript of a dialogue from the 2026 Utopia Reader's Day event. Chen Jiaying, from a philosophical perspective, explores the relationship between cognition and being-in-the-world, arguing that cognition stems from desire and can only be formed within specific contexts, with objectivity being 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.' Luo Xin responds from a historical viewpoint, emphasizing that historical research pursues truth while acknowledging its own limitations, and that the greatest value of the humanities lies in the process—cultivating judgment and the ability to ask questions. Zhou Sicheng raises the sharp question of whether AI can achieve 'the most objective cognition without being-in-the-world.' The three scholars agree that AI can provide brilliant answers and synthesize existing knowledge, but cannot truly pose new questions. In an era of AI as a 'deus ex machina,' the core value of philosophy and history lies in cultivating the human ability to ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments. The dialogue also touches on the plurality of historical interpretation, the differences in objectivity between the social and natural sciences, and the shortcomings of Chinese education in terms of intellectual depth.

mainPoints.point: Cognition stems from the desires of beings-in-the-world; objectivity is 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.'
mainPoints.explanation: Chen Jiaying argues that living beings develop cognition because they have desires; cognition is not about receiving all information but about simplifying complexity. Objectivity is not a starting point but a process, akin to 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.'

mainPoints.point: The greatest value of the humanities lies in the process, not in reaching a single conclusion.
mainPoints.explanation: Luo Xin points out that historical research pursues truth while being aware of its own limitations. Cultivating a sense of history, judgment, and the ability to ask questions is more important than reaching perfect conclusions; the process itself is education.

mainPoints.point: AI can mimic the results of cognition but cannot pose truly new questions.
mainPoints.explanation: Chen Jiaying believes that the way AI operates is fundamentally different from human cognition, though the results are highly similar. Luo Xin adds that AI is an 'extremely low-cost, interdisciplinary senior consultant' that can synthesize existing knowledge but cannot ask original questions like Chen Yinke could.

mainPoints.point: In the age of AI, the core value of philosophy and history is to cultivate judgment and narrative ability.
mainPoints.explanation: The three scholars agree that AI can provide brilliant answers, but the ability to truly ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments still belongs only to humans, and this ability can only be cultivated through humanistic training.

keyQuotes: AI can provide brilliant answers, but the ability to truly ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments still belongs only to beings-in-the-world, who have desires, who hesitate, and who persist.
Life is a series of increasingly pure efforts.

AI is like a learned person who has never existed in history... In terms of creative advancement, there is nothing admirable about it. The questions AI raises are actually questions others have already asked.
The objectivity that historians pursue has little to do with their specific personal feelings... This is a starting point for historical research.

relatedArticles.title: "She Is the Ceiling of Text Among Chinese Actresses"
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through the lens of non-fiction writer Yang Suqiu, this article offers a deep reading of Joan Chen's memoir "Catfish," analyzing the spiritual inheritance, career pursuits, and emotional bonds of three generations of women in the interstices of time, while exploring the unique value of female memory, friendship, and intergenerational relationships.

relatedArticles.title: Seven Misconceptions About Taste and Its Essence
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: The author systematically refutes seven common misconceptions about taste, citing multiple philosophers, and ultimately defines taste as 'trained perception × the judgment to say no × the courage to bear the consequences.'

relatedArticles.title: 167. How Would Plato, Rousseau, Hayek, and Arendt Explain the Algorithm Age? | Cross-Podcast Collaboration with Du Shu Bu Cheng Lin
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: From Plato's cave allegory to Arendt's public space, how the philosophical frameworks of four thinkers help us understand the cognitive limitations, erosion of public space, and challenges of self-expression in the algorithm age.

relatedArticles.title: In the End, People Must Learn to Live with the Past
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Using the personal experience of an East German woman as a thread, this article tells a non-fiction story interwoven with love, betrayal, collapsed faith, and historical upheaval, exploring how individuals reconcile with the past amid the ruins of the Cold War.

relatedArticles.title: This Is the Top Skill That Humans Can Never Be Replaced By AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues from the perspectives of philosophical history and cognitive science that tacit knowledge (intuition, taste, judgment that cannot be articulated) is the core ability that AI cannot replace, and the competition between humans and AI is essentially a race in the speed of producing tacit knowledge.

relatedArticles.title: Dialogue with Wang Fang: Calling Yourself a "Workhorse" Only Worsens Your Workplace Situation
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Wang Fang, a psychology professor at Beijing Normal University, points out that calling yourself a "workhorse" worsens your workplace situation. Psychology is not a tool-like "life guide" but a pair of "glasses" that helps people see their own circumstances clearly. Even within structural constraints, individuals can still maintain awareness and choice.

relatedArticles.title: Liu Sola: Who Is She, Really?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article traces Liu Sola's跨界 life from a literary pioneer in the 1980s to an international musician, revealing her constant refusal to be labeled and her fluid state of being, while exploring her insights on selfhood and authenticity for contemporary readers.

relatedArticles.title: A Serious Discussion: How Much of Our Skills Can Skill Actually Distill? | Hao's Trend Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the capability boundaries of AI Agent Skills, pointing out that while they excel at encoding explicit rules and knowledge routing, they cannot capture the tacit intuition and utility judgment that human experts rely on in complex decision-making.

relatedArticles.title: A Psychiatrist's 30 Years: How Do People Coexist with Pain?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Senior psychiatrist Jiang Tao, drawing on 35 years of clinical experience and his new book "Settle the Heart", deeply explores the medical nature of mental illness, social stigma, and the possibility of coexisting with pain.

relatedArticles.title: What Are We Really Nostalgic For?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Using the phenomenon of 'Yugonostalgia' as a case study and drawing on the theoretical framework of restorative and reflective nostalgia, this article analyzes how individuals, amid historical ruptures and nationalist discourse, seek identity and emotional healing by longing for the past.
